evaluation.positioning_hook: A weary orbital depot crew discovers their station is treating them as insured assets while reality itself starts compressing around one man the system has decided is the problem.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean commercial engine: a workplace sci-fi disaster that turns into a survival thriller with a strong corporate-horror hook. The audience is narrower than a four-quadrant space adventure, but the insurance/asset angle and escalating station collapse give it a clear genre buyer.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early: a crew on an orbital depot learns they are literally insured assets, then the station begins failing in ways that make the premise feel both specific and legible. The script keeps the central idea visible through the Sim-Gate, the valuation matrix, and the orbital decay reveal.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Miller, Sarah, Vance, and Dr. Aris each have a distinct operating mode, and the script gives them friction that feels playable. Miller is the anchor, but the ensemble is strongest when the crew’s different responses to corporate dehumanization collide.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The insurance-as-human-resource-management idea, the Sim-Gate rendering threat, and the final preservation-room reveal are all confident, ownable choices. The script is willing to go abstract and uncanny without losing the workplace logic underneath it.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: Once the engineer dies in the Sim-Gate and the crew sees the valuation matrix, the story keeps escalating with clear cause-and-effect: contamination, containment, orbital decay, decompression, crash, escape. The back half is especially propulsive because each new system failure narrows the options.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script feels fresh because it fuses corporate exploitation, hard-sci-fi infrastructure, and body-horror logic into one escalating machine. The idea that the system learns the threat rather than just contains it gives the premise a memorable, inevitable quality.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The depot feels lived-in and operational: shift fatigue, legacy systems, maintenance trusses, EVA procedures, insurance language, and corporate hierarchy all create a believable social ecosystem. The world is story-generating because every subsystem can fail and every role has a place in the machine.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually specific: deadpan workplace banter, procedural tech detail, and creeping cosmic dread all coexist without flattening each other. The final monochrome preservation-room coda sharpens the script’s identity rather than just ending on a twist.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There’s more going on than the immediate survival plot: identity, labor, corporate ownership, and the idea of being “learned” by a system all suggest deeper thematic layers. The script doesn’t over-explain those layers, which gives it room to resonate beyond the immediate plot mechanics.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The crew dynamics are strong enough that multiple pairings generate material: Miller/Sarah, Miller/Vance, Vance/Dixon, Riggs/Aris, and the group as a whole under pressure. The script repeatedly uses banter, distrust, and shared labor to keep the ensemble alive.

lead_characters.name: Miller McCord
lead_characters.hook: The depot’s most emotionally sealed operator, Miller is the kind of man who survives by staying precise, quiet, and one step ahead of panic. He knows the system is lying before anyone else does, and once the crew is reduced to assets on a contract, his restraint becomes the thing holding the group together.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael B. Jordan in a pressure-cooker lead role: contained authority, buried grief, and the slow reveal of a man whose stillness is doing violent work. It gives an actor the chance to play command, suspicion, and moral clarity without ever turning into a speech machine.

lead_characters.name: Sarah Beaumont
lead_characters.hook: Sarah is the crew’s sharpest social reader, the one who can clock the lie in the room before the system does. She’s funny, blunt, and emotionally braver than the men around her, which makes her both a pressure valve and a moral accelerant.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Jurnee Smollett in Lovecraft Country or Jodie Comer in The Last Duel a lot to do: intelligence, bite, and emotional authority inside a genre engine. It offers a performer a chance to steal scenes by being the first person to say the thing everyone else is circling.

lead_characters.name: Vance Matheson
lead_characters.hook: Vance is the anxious systems brain who talks fast, thinks faster, and starts to fray as the station’s logic collapses around him. He’s comic until he isn’t, and the script uses that shift to make him feel like the crew member most likely to crack under the math.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong character-actor territory in the vein of Paul Dano in The Fabelmans or Jesse Plemons in Game Night: a role that lets an actor toggle between dry humor, panic, and technical brilliance. The appeal is the visible unraveling of a smart man who can see the disaster but not outrun it.

lead_characters.name: Riggs
lead_characters.hook: Riggs is the depot’s managerial face: tired, evasive, and committed to the language of contract and compliance even as reality starts to fail. He reads like a middle manager until the script reveals him as one of the system’s most unsettling embodiments of corporate indifference.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Bryan Cranston did in Breaking Bad’s early corporate/authority scenes or what John Turturro does best: make bureaucracy feel predatory. The showcase is in the gradual reveal that his blandness is not neutrality but a weapon.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Patricia Aris
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Aris is the one person on the station who seems to understand the machinery and the human cost at the same time. Dry, unsentimental, and quietly defiant, she becomes the script’s most overtly rebellious adult in the room.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prestige-supporting territory in the vein of Frances McDormand in Three Billboards or Annette Bening in 20th Century Women: an adult woman with authority, wit, and a refusal to be managed. It gives an actor a chance to play competence as rebellion.

lead_characters.name: Dixon
lead_characters.hook: Dixon is the crew’s loudest skeptic and most instinctive survivor, the guy who jokes through danger until the danger gets too real to joke about. He’s abrasive, funny, and physically present in a way that keeps the ensemble from becoming too cerebral.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the same kind of scene-stealing lift Walton Goggins gets in ensemble genre work: attitude, rhythm, and a real turn when the stakes spike. It’s a great part for someone who can make defiance feel like a coping mechanism.

lead_characters.name: Hendrix
lead_characters.hook: Hendrix is the giant systems specialist whose body is always slightly at odds with the station’s geometry. He’s dry, smart, and physically memorable, and the script uses him as both comic texture and tragic proof that the environment is already closing in.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a strong physical signature and then lets the performance deepen into dread, similar to what Dave Bautista has done in genre work. The showcase is the contrast between his size, his wit, and the vulnerability of being crushed by the machine.

lead_characters.name: Robert
lead_characters.hook: Robert is one of the station’s working hands, a practical presence who helps make the depot feel like a real workplace rather than a concept. He’s less defined than the core quartet, but he gives the ensemble needed operational texture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is solid working-actor material: the kind of role that benefits from a performer who can make routine feel lived-in and then sell the shock when the environment turns lethal. It’s not a fireworks part, but it is a credible, grounded one.

lead_characters.name: Technician
lead_characters.hook: The Technician is the final, unnerving reveal: a bland, managerial figure who treats the surviving crew like inventory in a preservation room. He’s not a villain in the usual sense; he’s the script’s coldest expression of process.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-reveal role that lets an actor land a whole movie’s thesis in a few scenes, similar to the authority-without-emotion energy of a great Twilight Zone or Black Mirror antagonist. The showcase is in making bureaucratic calm feel more horrifying than overt menace.

casting_characteristics: one lead Black male in his 40s

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: mostly interior with limited exterior EVA sequences
notable_requirements: EVA truss and exterior hull work

technical.vfx_details: Orbital exterior, station collapse, environment-print distortions, holographic interfaces, decompression effects, and the final preservation-room visual language require substantial but contained VFX.
technical.sfx_needs: practical decompression, lighting failure, heat/breach effects, suit compression, and station-system failure beats.

rights_flags.detail: Andy Williams' 'How Long Has This Been Going On?' is specifically named in the preservation-room coda.
The closing super references Serling, Matheson, Beaumont, O'Bannon, Gilligan, Mann, Scott, Cameron, Nolan, Bigelow, Fuqua, and Coogler by name.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best positioned as a streamer-first or specialty theatrical sci-fi thriller.

budget.note: The depot interiors are controllable, but the EVA exterior, station-collapse sequence, decompression, and final collapse/pod escape push this above a simple contained indie.

casting.note: The lead needs a strong Black male actor in his 40s who can play restraint, command, and dread, and Hendrix adds a very tall physical requirement that narrows the supporting search.

development.note: The script’s abstract final movement and the preservation-room reveal are distinctive, but they also ask a buyer to trust a concept that gets increasingly metaphysical after a very concrete survival setup.

comp_set.title: Life
comp_set.why_it_comps: A contained space-disaster thriller where the environment becomes the antagonist and the crew’s survival logic drives the tension.

comp_set.title: The Thing
comp_set.why_it_comps: The paranoia, contamination logic, and locked-workplace dread echo the way this script turns a crew into suspects inside a hostile system.

comp_set.title: Aniara
comp_set.why_it_comps: The orbital setting, existential drift, and corporate/structural hopelessness place it in the same bleak sci-fi lane.

comp_set.title: Moon
comp_set.why_it_comps: A solitary, industrial sci-fi environment with a strong identity crisis at the center and a controlled production footprint.

comp_set.title: Event Horizon
comp_set.why_it_comps: The escalation from technical malfunction to full-on cosmic horror gives it that same hard-turn into nightmare territory.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like smart, claustrophobic sci-fi thrillers with corporate horror, survival stakes, and a strong ensemble.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly male-skewing but viable for genre-savvy women; premium-streaming and specialty-theatrical audience with strong sci-fi/horror overlap.

budget_tier.note: Controlled interiors keep it in range, but the orbital exterior work, VFX distortions, and station-collapse finale push it into mid-budget genre territory.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where concept-forward sci-fi meets adult character tension and a contained production footprint. The script has enough scale to feel eventful, but enough interiority and control to appeal to buyers who want a smart genre swing rather than a tentpole.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the world is strong, but there is no clear sequel or spinoff vector with a supporting character deep enough to anchor a separate project.

strengths.what_it_means: It gives the movie a clean commercial thesis: corporate dehumanization made literal, which is easy to pitch and easy to remember. That makes it attractive to streamer genre buyers and actors who want a role with social bite, not just survival mechanics.
strengths.evidence: The crew valuation matrix, the 'asset' language, and Riggs treating crew members as reimbursable losses turn the premise into a workplace nightmare.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble has real operating friction.
strengths.what_it_means: The script can generate scenes from character conflict, not just plot events, which is what makes contained genre features feel bigger than their footprint. That’s the kind of ensemble energy that appeals to directors and actors looking for a playable group dynamic.
strengths.evidence: Miller’s restraint, Sarah’s bluntness, Vance’s systems anxiety, Dixon’s defiance, and Dr. Aris’s dry authority all create distinct rhythms in the same room.

strengths.what_it_means: Most of the movie lives in controlled interiors with a limited number of recurring spaces, which makes the concept feel premium without requiring tentpole spend. That is exactly the kind of production profile buyers like when they want scale on a contained budget.
strengths.evidence: The depot, commons, control rooms, truss, lifepod platform, and preservation-room coda do most of the work.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The final reveal reframes the whole movie.
strengths.what_it_means: The preservation-room coda turns the survival story into something colder and more unsettling, which gives the script aftertaste and conversation value. That kind of ending is useful in the market because it makes the movie feel like more than a one-note genre exercise.
strengths.evidence: The monochrome Technician, the archive drawers labeled with crew names, and the 'your turn' line land the thesis with a final sting.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The station itself behaves like a character.
strengths.what_it_means: A setting that can fail, compress, misread, and hunt gives the movie a built-in escalation engine and a strong visual identity. Buyers respond to worlds that generate plot on their own, especially in sci-fi horror.
strengths.evidence: The Sim-Gate distortions, shrinking air clearance, orbital decay, and decompression breach all come from the depot’s own systems turning hostile.

whats_special.headline: This is a smart, pitchable sci-fi thriller with a strong commercial spine: corporate dehumanization made literal, a contained production footprint, and an ensemble that can carry tension scene by scene. The movie feels like a premium-streaming or specialty-theatrical buy because it delivers scale, dread, and a memorable thesis without needing tentpole economics.

items.area: The final act turns abstract fast.
items.detail: The move from station-collapse survival into the monochrome preservation-room coda is striking, but it shifts the movie from concrete thriller logic into a more metaphysical register very late. That’s a real buyer conversation because the ending is memorable, but it also changes the promise of the piece after the audience has been trained on procedural danger.

items.area: The lead is more functional than revelatory on the page.
items.detail: Miller is a strong anchor, but much of his power comes from withholding and competence rather than a deeply surprising personal contradiction. That keeps the role playable, but it also means the movie’s emotional center depends heavily on casting and performance rather than page-level volatility.

items.area: The supporting cast is vivid, but unevenly deep.
items.detail: Sarah, Vance, Dixon, and Dr. Aris all have clear voices, but some of the secondary crew members function more as operational texture than fully durable character engines. That matters in a multi-protag ensemble because the movie’s relationship density is strongest in the core quartet and thinner outside it.

items.area: The VFX burden is concentrated in the back half.
items.detail: The Sim-Gate distortions, orbital exterior work, decompression breach, station collapse, and final pod escape all stack into the same stretch of the movie. That’s manageable, but it means the production has to protect the finale carefully or the script’s biggest selling points get expensive fast.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is tonal and structural: it starts as a hard-edged workplace survival thriller and ends in a more surreal, archival nightmare mode. That’s a strong signature, but it will be the first thing buyers weigh against the movie’s otherwise clean, contained genre packaging.
